steps.prompt: Board C-114 extracted 412 ug of sodium chloride equivalent into the test solvent. Subtract the 6 ug method blank and divide by the 192 cm2 board area. What is the result, in ug/cm2? Two decimals.
hints: The blank is the solvent, the container and the handling, not the board.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2.11 ug/cm2 — four times the customer's limit, and the blank was worth 3 % of it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the blank first, then divide by the board area.
steps.explanation: 406 ug over 192 cm2 is 2.11 ug/cm2 of sodium chloride equivalent. The blank looks like bookkeeping and is not: at a 0.5 ug/cm2 limit the 6 ug blank is worth 0.03 ug/cm2, and on a small board it can be worth more than the margin. Done the other way round — 412 / 192 — the answer is 2.15, a 2 % error here and a much larger one on a 30 cm2 assembly. A ROSE number without its area and its blank is not a measurement, it is a reading.

steps.prompt: This customer's specification sets 0.5 ug/cm2, not the 1.56 reference value. What is one board allowed to carry in total, in micrograms, on its 192 cm2?
hints: The limit is per square centimetre, so multiply it by the area.
96 ug for the whole board.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 96 ug for the whole board — C-114 brought 406 ug net into the cell.
steps.feedbackWrong: Multiply the per-area limit by the area; do not compare a total with a per-area limit.
steps.explanation: 0.5 ug/cm2 on 192 cm2 allows 96 ug in the extraction cell; C-114 came in with 406 ug net. The same liquid that fails this board would pass it against the reference 1.56, which allows 299.5 ug, so the customer specification is not a formality — it is the limit that decides. A per-area limit and a total are different numbers, and the line compares them with each other more often than anyone would like to believe.

steps.prompt: The customer's spec says 0.5 ug/cm2, the reference value is 1.56, and the twelve study boards sit at 1.00. Which statement is right?

options.text: The boards pass, because 1.00 is below the 1.56 reference value and that is the limit that applies.
The boards fail the customer's 0.5 and would pass the reference 1.56; the customer limit governs, so the process is not in control for this build.
The boards are acceptable because the average is below the reference limit.
The 1.56 value is a legal maximum, so a customer cannot ask for less.

hints: The lesson treats 1.56 as the default that applies when nobody specified anything.
1.00 against 0.5 is a fail; 1.00 against 1.56 is a pass.
Decide which limit governs before deciding pass or fail.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 1.00 fails the 0.5 customer limit and passes the 1.56 reference — the customer limit governs, so this process is not capable for this build.
steps.feedbackWrong: One measurement cannot be compared with two limits and accepted if it clears either of them.
steps.explanation: 1.56 ug/cm2 is what applies when nothing tighter has been specified; the lesson lists 1.0, 0.75 and 0.5 as the tiers customers write for telecom, aerospace and medical work. Here the customer wrote 0.5, so 0.5 governs. A process mean of 1.00 sits at twice the allowed level, and the whole distribution is above it — this is not a marginal call but a process that was never qualified against the limit it is measured against. That is the expensive form of the mistake: a line that has been passing itself against the wrong number, on paper, for a year.

steps.prompt: The line manager calls C-114 an outlier: one board at 2.11 against a mean of 1.00. What does the C-114 data actually show?

options.text: An outlier, to be reported as an excursion, with the process left alone.

Not an outlier but what a whole-board average does to a local pocket: the 20 x 20 mm site under the BGA extracted 12 ug on its own, which is 3.00 ug/cm2 on the site while the rest of the board sits near 0.5.
An invalid site test, because ROSE is only defined per whole board.
A board to reclean and retest, with no further action.

hints: Work the site out: 12 ug on 4 cm2.
Divide the whole-board result by 192 and it cannot see a 4 cm2 pocket.
A residue pocket is hidden by the area it is averaged over.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 3.00 ug/cm2 on the site against 2.11 for the board — the residue is a pocket under the BGA, and the average is the wrong instrument.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the site result by the site area, then compare it with the board average.
steps.explanation: 12 ug on 4 cm2 is 3.00 ug/cm2 at the site. If the rest of the board sits near 0.5, then 4 cm2 out of 192 is producing almost the entire whole-board figure of 2.11 — which is exactly how a wash that cannot reach under a 256-ball BGA looks in a number that passes. The lesson is direct about it: averaging hides a local residue pocket, so high-risk areas are tested separately. The dangerous version of this is not the board that fails, it is the board whose average passes while a site fails.

steps.prompt: C-121 extracted 171.1 ug with the same 6 ug blank and the same 192 cm2. What is its result, in ug/cm2? Two decimals.
hints: Same blank, same area; only the extracted mass changes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.86 ug/cm2 — 72 % over the customer limit and comfortably inside the reference.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the blank, then divide by 192.
steps.explanation: 0.86 ug/cm2 is the most instructive number in the case. Against the reference 1.56 this board passes with 45 % of the allowance unused; against the customer's 0.5 it is 72 % over. Same measurement, same instrument, opposite decisions, and the only difference is which limit the line writes on the report. A cleanliness result quoted without its limit is not a result.

steps.prompt: The process runs at 1.00 ug/cm2 with a standard deviation of 0.11. To have no more than 0.1 % of boards above the customer's 0.50 limit, what mean would the process have to hold, in ug/cm2? Two decimals.
hints: Work back from the limit: 0.1 % in one tail is 3.09 standard deviations.
needed mean = 0.50 - 3.09 x 0.11.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.16 ug/cm2 — the process is at 1.00, six times the mean it would have to hold.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the allowance from the limit; a wide spread does not become acceptable because the mean is high.
steps.explanation: A one-sided 0.1 % tail sits 3.09 standard deviations below the limit, so the mean would have to hold 0.50 - 3.09 x 0.11 = 0.16 ug/cm2. The process is at 1.00, six times that. This is the number that turns a complaint into a project: the gap is not closed by better sampling or a stricter test, it is closed by cleaning chemistry, rinse quality, bath life and the fixtures that stop the wash reaching under the BGA. Reporting the study mean against the reference limit, for a customer whose limit is a third of it, is how a process spends a year looking healthy while every board it ships is out of specification.

steps.prompt: A board extracts 198 ug and passes ROSE, and a 20 x 20 mm site under a connector extracts nothing. Which result should block the coating?

options.text: The whole-board result: 198 ug less the 6 ug blank is 192 ug over 192 cm2, which is 1.00 ug/cm2 against this customer's 0.5.
Neither: ROSE is a gate and both results are under their limits.
The whole-board result is an artefact of the blank and should be corrected upwards to 1.03, a pass against the reference.
Visual inspection, because neither test measures what blocks coating.

hints: Do the arithmetic on 198 ug before comparing anything.
(198 - 6) / 192 = 1.00, exactly twice the customer's limit.
A clean site does not rescue the rest of the board.
steps.feedbackCorrect: The whole-board result is 1.00 after the blank, twice the customer limit, and it blocks the coating whatever the site shows.
steps.feedbackWrong: Compare 1.00 with 0.5, not with 1.56, and remember that a clean site is evidence about 4 cm2 only.
steps.explanation: (198 - 6) / 192 = 1.00 ug/cm2 exactly, twice this customer's limit, so the board fails and coating it would seal the residue in. The site is clean because the residue is somewhere else; a clean site is evidence about 4 cm2 and nothing more. This is the mirror image of C-114 — there the average passed and the site failed, here the site passes and the average fails — and in both cases one number taken alone gives the wrong disposition. The rule that covers both is to test the high-risk sites separately and require every result to be under the governing limit before coating.

steps.prompt: A 90 um wet film is applied and the coating is 38 % solids. What is the dry film, and is it inside a 25-130 um qualification window?

options.text: 90 um, because the film thickness is what was applied, and that is inside the window.
34.2 um, which is inside the window but near its floor.
55.8 um, which is 90 um less the 38 % solids, inside the window.
237 um, because the solids are added rather than multiplied.

hints: The solvent leaves during cure; what stays is the solids fraction.
Multiply the wet film by 0.38.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 34.2 um dry from a 90 um wet film — inside the window and close to the floor.
steps.feedbackWrong: The solids fraction multiplies the wet film; it does not divide it.
steps.explanation: 90 um wet at 38 % solids leaves 34.2 um dry, inside the 25-130 um window and close enough to the floor that a 60 um wet film would fall to 22.8 um and out of it. The window is a qualification range, not a target, and the criterion that matters for protection is a minimum. Wet-film measurement before cure is the only cheap chance to catch this: after cure the thickness is measured destructively on coupons, so the trend across coupons matters more than any single reading.

steps.prompt: Coating is applied at 35 um dry over the area that is not masked: 192 cm2 less 16.0 for the connector, 3.0 for the test points and 0.377 under the BGA. At 38 % solids, what wet volume has to be dispensed, in millilitres? Two decimals.
hints: Coated area = 192 - 19.377 cm2.
Dry volume = area x thickness, with 35 um written as 0.0035 cm.
Wet volume = dry volume / 0.38, and 1 cm3 = 1 mL.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 1.59 mL of wet coating — the number the dispenser program needs.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the dry volume by the solids fraction; multiplying gives the solids, not the liquid.
steps.explanation: The coated area is 172.623 cm2, the dry film volume 0.604 cm3, and at 38 % solids the wet volume is 1.59 mL. A program that dispenses 0.60 mL paints a third of the board. The masked area is the part that is easy to get wrong, because it is not just the connector: the BGA needs masking of its own, and the test points are the area nobody remembers until the fixture cannot probe the board. That is what coating work really turns on — the areas that must stay bare decide the area that gets covered, and the volume follows.

steps.prompt: The customer asks for the evidence that this build is clean and coated. What is the package?

options.text: The ROSE result per board, because the pass limit is the whole criterion.

Per board: the extracted mass, the blank, the area, the method, the limit with its source, and the site results for the high-risk areas; plus coating thickness on coupons with the wet-to-dry arithmetic, the masked areas, and the disposition of the boards that failed.
A certificate stating that the process is qualified to IPC-CC-830.
The ion chromatography results, because they identify the ions and are therefore stricter than ROSE.

hints: Ask what a second engineer would need in order to recompute a decision.
The limit, its source, the area and the blank are all part of the number.
The disposition of the failures is evidence too, not an admission.
steps.feedbackCorrect: The record that carries its area, blank, limit and source, the local sites, the coating arithmetic and the failure dispositions is the one that can be audited.
steps.feedbackWrong: A certificate and a single number both describe the process; the record has to let somebody check it.
steps.explanation: The record has to answer the questions the numbers raise: which area the result applies to, which blank was subtracted, which limit governs and where it came from, what the high-risk sites measured on their own, how the coating thickness was derived from the wet film, which areas were masked, and what happened to the boards that failed. IPC-CC-830 qualifies a coating material and 2.3.25 defines the test; neither tells this customer whether this build is acceptable, and that judgement is what the package has to carry.

A per-area limit converted to a total for the board in question
The governing limit identified among reference, customer and process mean
Local site computed and the board average shown to hide it
One measurement against both limits, and the decision shown to depend on which is written
Process capability worked from the distribution, not the mean
A clean site and a failing average both resolved to a disposition
Wet-to-dry film arithmetic and the coating volume for the unmasked area
Evidence package carries area, blank, limit source, sites, coating arithmetic and dispositions

cases.title: Moisture breach: the BGA reel sat in a 7 % RH cabinet
scenario: Board X's 256-ball BGA comes in on MSL 4 tape and reel. The reel was opened 58 h ago and went straight into the storage dry cabinet. The cabinet log shows 7 % RH for the whole period; the setpoint in the procedure is 5 %.
During the second shift a feeder was loaded and the reel sat on the machine for 6 h before the line went down. Reflow of that build is planned 10 h from now.
Decide the disposition. The lesson is explicit that a cabinet above the dry-storage requirement does not stop the clock, and that a tape-and-reel bake has a hard temperature ceiling.

dataFiles.name: msl-log.csv
dataFiles.content:

steps.prompt: What is the J-STD-033 floor life for MSL 4, in hours at the reference condition?
hints: The values in the course run 168 h, 72 h, 48 h, 24 h down the levels.
MSL 4 is the third value in that sequence.
MSL 4 = 72 h.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 72 h — the number the whole disposition hangs on.
steps.feedbackWrong: This is a table lookup, not an arithmetic result: MSL 4 is 72 h.
steps.explanation: MSL 4 has 72 h of floor life at 30 °C / 60 % RH. MSL 3 is 168 h and MSL 5 is 48 h, which is why the levels are always quoted with their value.

steps.prompt: How many hours count against that floor life? Add the bag-open period and the time on the open feeder.
hints: A 7 % RH cabinet is above the 5 % requirement, so the cabinet time is not suspended.
The 6 h on the feeder is outside the cabinet entirely.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 64 h counted — the cabinet gave no credit at 7 % RH.
steps.feedbackWrong: Every hour counts here: the cabinet was not compliant, so nothing is discounted.
steps.explanation: A cabinet at 7 % RH is above the 5 % dry-storage requirement, so exposure keeps accumulating; the 6 h on the open feeder adds on top. 58 + 6 = 64 h of a 72 h budget.

steps.prompt: How much floor life is left for the BGA reel, in hours?
hints: Subtract the counted exposure from the floor life.
72 h minus 64 h.
8 h remain, against a reflow planned in 10 h.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 8 h left, and the reflow is 10 h away — the reel cannot simply proceed.
steps.feedbackWrong: Floor life minus counted exposure, in hours.
steps.explanation: 72 - 64 = 8 h remain, but the planned reflow is 10 h away. The batch is 2 h short, so the decision is bake or reschedule, not release.

steps.prompt: The cabinet logged 7 % RH against a 5 % requirement. What does the course say that does to the clock?

options.text: It suspends the clock, because any dry cabinet below 10 % RH is equivalent to sealed dry pack.
It slows the clock, but 5 % RH or less is the condition that suspends it, so this storage gave no credit.
It resets the clock, because the parts were dry when they went in.
It has no effect either way; only the bag seal matters.

hints: The lesson was corrected on exactly this point: 10 % RH is not the requirement.
5 % RH or less is what stops moisture uptake; above it the budget keeps shrinking, just more slowly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 7 % RH slows the clock but does not suspend it, so no credit was given.
steps.feedbackWrong: Look at which relative humidity the lesson calls the requirement, not which is common on a cheap cabinet.
steps.explanation: Below 5 % RH the device stops gaining moisture, so the exposure clock is suspended. A 10 % cabinet is common and slows the clock rather than stopping it; at 7 % the parts were outside the requirement, so the full 64 h counts. The 10 % form is a mitigation for devices with budget to spare, never a substitute for the requirement.

steps.prompt: The reel needs a bake. What is the maximum temperature the tape and reel may see, in °C?
hints: Carrier tape and cover tape soften and deform when they get hot.
The lesson gives a fixed ceiling for tape and reel, not a range.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 40 °C — and at 40 °C the bake takes days, not hours.
steps.feedbackWrong: The value is a fixed ceiling in the lesson, well below the 125 °C tray bake.
steps.explanation: Tape and reel must not be baked above 40 °C because the carrier and cover tape deform. At that temperature the table runs to days for a thin body, which is why the 40 °C route does not fit a 10 h window.

steps.prompt: The reflow is 10 h away and a 40 °C bake will not finish in time. Which route does the lesson support?

options.text: Bake the reel at 125 °C now and accept some tape deformation.
De-reel into trays, bake the loose parts at the permitted higher temperature, then re-reel; or move the build inside the remaining floor life.
Skip the bake and raise the reflow peak by 10 °C to drive the moisture out.
Run the reel as-is and inspect the BGA after reflow.

hints: Which constraint is physical and which is scheduling?
The tape ceiling is a material limit; the schedule is not. The lesson offers de-reeling and rescheduling.
De-reel to a carrier that tolerates 125 °C, or move the reflow inside the 8 h.
steps.feedbackCorrect: De-reel and bake at the higher temperature, or move the build inside the remaining floor life.
steps.feedbackWrong: The lesson never trades a material limit for a schedule.
steps.explanation: Baking a reel at 125 °C destroys the carrier tape, and raising the peak adds thermal stress without removing moisture. The two supported routes are de-reeling to a carrier rated for the 125 °C bake, or rescheduling the build inside the 8 h that remain. Reflowing an unbaked MSL 4 batch and inspecting afterwards turns a known risk into a detection gamble.

Exposure counted with no credit for a non-compliant cabinet
Remaining life computed and compared with the reflow schedule
7 % RH judged against the 5 % requirement
Tape-and-reel bake ceiling known

cases.title: Profile validation: Board X runs a 248 °C peak
scenario: Board X is a 1.6 mm six-layer board with heavy ground planes and a large BGA. The thermal survey from the worst-case site gives the profile in the data file: 25 to 150 °C in 60 s, soak 150 to 190 °C for 90 s, 65 s above 219 °C, peak 248 °C, and cooling from 248 to 100 °C in 40 s.

Paste is SAC305. The paste window for this board is 60-90 s above liquidus (IPC-7530B guidance is 30-90 s; the datasheet narrows it). The peak is judged against a ceiling, not a target: the J-STD-020 classification temperature for a large package at 1.6-2.5 mm is 250 °C, while the course's typical production band is 235-245 °C.
Validate the profile, compute the margins, and decide whether it can be released with a documentation note or must be changed.

steps.prompt: What is the ramp rate from 25 °C to 150 °C, in °C/s?
hints: Rate is a temperature difference over a time.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2.08 °C/s — inside the 1-3 °C/s guidance.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the rise by the seconds, not the other way round.
steps.explanation: 125 °C in 60 s gives 2.08 °C/s, which sits inside the 1-3 °C/s guidance the course takes from IPC-7530. This is the figure the m06 lesson works, and it matters because a ramp that is too fast drives tombstoning on the 0402s.

steps.prompt: The profile gives 65 s above 219 °C. Against the paste datasheet window of 60-90 s, how many seconds of margin are there at the lower end?
hints: The window opens at 60 s.
65 s minus 60 s.
5 s of margin.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 5 s above the lower bound — inside the window, with little margin.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the window minimum from the measured time above liquidus.
steps.explanation: 65 s clears the 60 s floor of the paste window by 5 s. The course treats that as passing but thin: a slower line or a colder zone could drop the board below the window without anyone changing the recipe.

steps.prompt: The survey ran three thermocouples. Using thermocouples.csv, what is the peak-to-peak spread across the board, in °C?
hints: Spread is the hottest site minus the coldest, not a distance to a limit.
Hottest is the 0402 near the edge, coldest is the BGA centre joint.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 12 °C across the board — and the mean of the three is the 248 °C the single-point profile reported.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the coldest peak from the hottest; ignore the middle site.
steps.explanation: 254 - 242 = 12 °C. The mean of the three sites is 248 °C, exactly the peak the single-point profile reported, which is why one thermocouple makes a graded board look uniform. The spread is the finding: 242 °C at the BGA centre is 3 °C under the paste band top, and 254 °C at the 0402 near the edge is 9 °C over it and 4 °C over the 250 °C classification ceiling for a large package. The single average of 248 °C sits inside the band and hides both facts, which is why the record has to carry the spread and not the average.

steps.prompt: Peak is 248 °C and the large-package classification temperature is 250 °C. What margin is left, in °C?
hints: Margin is limit minus measured, not measured minus limit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2 °C of margin to the classification limit.
steps.feedbackWrong: The limit is the upper number; subtract the measurement from it.
steps.explanation: 250 - 248 leaves 2 °C. The classification temperature is a ceiling for the package, so a 2 °C margin means any zone drift or heavier board can push the peak over it — worth a note in the profile record even though the profile passes.

steps.prompt: Cooling runs from 248 °C to 100 °C in 40 s. What is the cooling rate in °C/s?
hints: Same rate formula, with the drop as the temperature difference.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 3.7 °C/s — fast cooling, good for grain structure but hard on large components.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use the drop (148 °C) over the 40 s cooling window.
steps.explanation: 148 °C in 40 s is 3.7 °C/s. The course notes that cooling that fast is good for fine grain but raises the thermal gradient across a large BGA, so it is a parameter to record and watch rather than a defect.

steps.prompt: Which disposition does the three-site survey earn?

options.text: Reject: the 0402 near the edge peaks over the paste band and over the package ceiling, so the profile cannot be released as measured.
Accept and document: the average peak and the time above liquidus are inside their windows, so the spread is recorded as a note only.
Accept without comment: a profile only fails if the joints look wrong.
Reject: time above liquidus must always exceed 90 s on a heavy board.

hints: The average is not the finding: look at the hottest and the coldest site.
254 °C at the 0402 near the edge is above both the paste band top (245 °C) and the large-package ceiling (250 °C).
A profile is judged on the worst measured point, not on the mean, so it cannot be released as measured.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Reject and change: the hot corner exceeds the paste band and the package ceiling.
steps.feedbackWrong: Averaging the three sites hides the one that fails. Judge the worst point.
steps.explanation: 254 °C at the 0402 near the edge is 9 °C over the paste band top and 4 °C over the J-STD-020 ceiling for a large package, so the profile fails at that point however good the 248 °C average looks. Time above liquidus is inside its window at every site, and the BGA centre at 242 °C is fine, which is exactly why the failing corner has to be found from the survey rather than from a single thermocouple. This is the lesson the case is built on: a mean is not a measurement of the worst case.

steps.prompt: A first-principles check: the oven delivers about 100 W and the board's measured thermal mass is 90 J/K. What ramp rate does that predict, in °C/s?
hints: Ramp rate from heat input is power divided by thermal mass.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 1.1 °C/s predicted, against 2.08 °C/s measured.
steps.feedbackWrong: Power over thermal mass; the units work out to °C/s directly.
steps.explanation: 100 / 90 = 1.1 °C/s, roughly half the measured ramp. The model is a sanity check, not an oracle: the real oven adds zone power and the board receives radiated heat, so a measured rate above the model is expected — but a factor of two is worth checking before the model is used to set a recipe.

steps.prompt: What should be done with the factor-of-two gap between the model and the measurement?

options.text: Trust the model: the measured thermocouple must be wrong.
Trust the measurement and record the model's assumptions as unvalidated for this board; re-measure a second worst-case site before using the model to predict zone settings.
Average the two values and use that as the ramp rate.
Ignore both and use the paste datasheet ramp figure.

hints: A thermocouple on the worst-case site is direct evidence; a lumped model is an estimate.
The lesson's own wording is to treat the model as an estimate and verify against measurement.
Keep the measurement, flag the model, and take a second site.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Keep the measurement, mark the model unvalidated for Board X, and check a second worst-case site.
steps.feedbackWrong: The question is which number is evidence and which is an assumption.
steps.explanation: The thermocouple is direct evidence; the 100 W / 90 J/K model is a lumped estimate that ignores radiation, zone coupling and board mass distribution. Averaging an estimate with a measurement produces a number with no physical meaning, and the datasheet ramp is a paste guideline, not this board's behaviour. Record the gap and re-measure a second site before the model is trusted.

steps.prompt: Using the measurement sheet, what is the nominal diametral clearance on J-01, in mm?
hints: Diametral clearance is the hole diameter minus the lead diameter.
Nominal hole 1.00 mm, nominal lead 0.60 mm.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.40 mm nominal, and the worst case is not that number.
steps.feedbackWrong: Take the finished hole diameter, not the drill diameter, then subtract the lead.
steps.explanation: 1.00 - 0.60 = 0.40 mm of diametral clearance. The radial clearance is half of that, 0.20 mm, which is the gap the solder has to climb through. The nominal case is the one the drawing shows; the joint that fails is rarely the nominal one.

steps.prompt: What is the worst-case tight diametral clearance, in mm: smallest finished hole against largest lead?
hints: Tight means the smallest hole against the largest lead.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.32 mm in the worst case, against 0.40 mm nominal.
steps.feedbackWrong: Both tolerances have to be used in their worst direction at the same time.
steps.explanation: A 0.95 mm hole with a 0.63 mm lead leaves 0.32 mm diametral, or 0.16 mm radial. The 0.08 mm of clearance lost to tolerance is a fifth of the nominal gap, and it is what separates a full barrel from a stalled one on a cold joint.

steps.prompt: What is that worst-case radial clearance, in mm?
hints: Radial clearance is half the diametral clearance.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.16 mm radially: the gap the solder draws through.
steps.feedbackWrong: Halve the diametral figure rather than repeating the subtraction.
steps.explanation: 0.32 / 2 = 0.16 mm radially. That is the capillary gap: wide enough to fill when hole and lead are clean and hot, narrow enough that a low top-side temperature stops the flow before the barrel fills.

steps.prompt: At nominal diameters, what is the annular volume the solder has to fill through the 1.6 mm board, in mm3? Use pi = 3.14159 and give two decimals.
hints: The annulus is the hole cylinder minus the lead cylinder.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.80 mm3 of annulus; the 75 % minimum asks for 0.60 mm3 of solder in it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the lead cross-section from the hole cross-section before multiplying by thickness.
steps.explanation: The hole holds pi * 0.5^2 * 1.6 = 1.26 mm3 and the lead takes pi * 0.3^2 * 1.6 = 0.45 mm3, leaving 0.80 mm3 of annulus. At the 75 % acceptance minimum the joint has to show 0.60 mm3 of solder to be acceptable at all.

steps.prompt: Cross-section shows 1.10 mm of fill on a 1.60 mm board. What is the vertical fill as a percentage? One decimal place.
hints: Fill percentage is filled depth divided by board thickness.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 68.75 %, under the 75 % minimum.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the filled depth by the full board thickness and scale to percent.
steps.explanation: 1.10 / 1.60 = 0.6875, so 68.75 %. The number matters because IPC-A-610 sets the minimum vertical barrel fill at 75 % for Class 2 and Class 3 alike; 68.75 % is a defect, not a cosmetic shortfall.

steps.prompt: The minimum is 75 % of the 1.60 mm board. How many millimetres of fill is J-01 short, in mm?
hints: Turn the percentage minimum into a depth first: 0.75 x 1.60 mm.
1.20 mm required, 1.10 mm measured.
0.10 mm short.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.10 mm short: a tenth of a millimetre, on a joint the operator called full.
steps.feedbackWrong: Convert the percentage to a depth before subtracting the measurement.
steps.explanation: The minimum depth is 0.75 * 1.60 = 1.20 mm and the joint has 1.10 mm, so it is 0.10 mm short. Ten hundredths of a millimetre decide between a released build and a rework, which is why fill is measured on a cross-section rather than judged from the solder-side fillet.

steps.prompt: What is the correct disposition of J-01?

options.text: Accept it: 68.75 % is close to 75 % and the joint is electrically connected.
Reject it against the 75 % minimum and rework it; every other joint in the sheet is judged on its own.
Accept it under the thermal-plane exception for 14 or more leads.
Accept it and raise the pot temperature by 10 °C so the next board fills further.

hints: The minimum for Class 2 and Class 3 is the same number; which is it?
The exception is for parts with 14 or more leads tied into internal thermal planes. The sheet records zero leads on a plane for this connector.
68.75 % is below 75 %, so the joint fails.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Reject J-01 and rework it: the 75 % minimum has no near-miss band.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which column in the sheet says whether this joint is acceptable?
steps.explanation: IPC-A-610 sets a 75 % minimum vertical fill for Class 2 and Class 3, and 68.75 % is below it. The 50 % / 1.2 mm figure is a documented exception for parts with fourteen or more leads tied into internal thermal planes; the sheet records zero leads on a plane, so the exception does not apply. Raising the pot temperature to rescue one joint changes every other joint on the board and leaves the mechanism in place.

steps.prompt: The other joints read 81.25 % and 78.13 %. What is the defensible reading of the sheet?

options.text: The build passes: the mean of the three joints is 76.04 %, above 75 %.
The build fails on J-01, and the sheet has to record each joint so the failing one cannot be averaged away.
The build passes because two joints out of three are above the minimum.
The build passes once J-01 is re-inspected by a second operator.

hints: Averaging is exactly the mistake this sheet exists to prevent.
One joint below the minimum is a defect on that joint, whatever the mean is.
Judge every joint: the average of acceptable and unacceptable is unacceptable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Judge joint by joint. J-01 fails, and a mean cannot repair it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Ask what the average would hide if the sheet recorded only a mean.
steps.explanation: The mean of 68.75, 81.25 and 78.13 is 76.04 %, which clears 75 % and hides the defect. Acceptance in IPC-A-610 is per joint, so the sheet must carry every joint; a summary that reports only an average cannot show which barrel is short. It is the same mistake as judging a reflow profile by its mean peak.

steps.prompt: What control actually addresses the short fill, given the wave record?

options.text: Raise the conveyor speed so the board spends less time in the wave.
Raise preheat so the top side of the hole reaches a temperature that lets the solder climb, and verify dwell and contact time against the equipment limits.
Add flux by hand at the connector before the wave.
Accept the fill and add 100 % X-ray inspection.

hints: Look at the wave record: contact time is 2.0 s, the bottom of the 2-4 s window the course teaches.
A short fill on a clean, wetted joint points at the thermal side of the process, not at solder volume.
Preheat and dwell decide whether the barrel fills; inspection only finds it later.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Raise preheat and check dwell against the equipment limits. Inspection after the fact does not fill a barrel.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which setting in wave-run.csv sits at the edge of its window?
steps.explanation: Contact time is 2.0 s, the very bottom of the 2-4 s window, and top-side preheat is 105 °C in a 90-120 °C band: both at the weak end for a connector that acts as a heat sink. Raising preheat and lengthening contact inside equipment limits addresses the mechanism. Speeding the conveyor shortens contact and makes it worse, and adding X-ray only proves the defect exists on every board after the cost is sunk.

Worst-case clearance built from both tolerances at once
Radial clearance derived from the diametral figure

Shortfall in millimetres derived from the percentage minimum

Each joint judged on its own, not on the average

scenario: The wave run that produced the m08 first article is recorded in wave-run.csv: rosin mildly activated flux, 105 °C top-side preheat, a 255 °C pot, a 50 mm wave and 1.5 m/min conveyor on a single-wave machine. The connector ran upstream.

steps.prompt: The wave is 50 mm wide and the conveyor runs at 1.5 m/min. What is the contact time, in seconds?
hints: Convert both lengths to the same unit before dividing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2.0 s: inside the 2-4 s window, but at the bottom of it.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the wave width in metres by the conveyor speed in metres per second.
steps.explanation: 0.050 m of wave over 0.025 m/s of board travel gives 2.0 s of contact. The course window is 2-4 s, so the run is legal, and the board passes through in the shortest time the window allows. For a connector that acts as a heat sink that is the first thing to look at, not the pot temperature.

steps.prompt: The pot runs at 255 °C. What is that above the SAC305 liquidus of 219 °C, in °C?
hints: Liquidus is the temperature the alloy must exceed, not a target.
36 °C above liquidus.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 36 °C above liquidus: the pot is hot, not cold.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the liquidus from the pot temperature, not the other way round.
steps.explanation: 255 - 219 = 36 °C. The course's own window for SAC305 pots is 250-260 °C, so the pot sits in the middle of it. The hypothesis that a cold pot explains the short fill is contradicted by the record before anyone touches a knob.

steps.prompt: The record is inside every window: pot 255 °C, contact 2.0 s, flux correct. Which pair of settings is actually weak for a heat-sinking connector?

options.text: The pot temperature and the flux type.
The top-side preheat, at 105 °C, and the contact time, at the floor of its window.
The conveyor speed, which is far too slow.
Nothing: the settings are fine and the defect must be incoming material.

hints: The course's preheat range is 90-120 °C top side; where in that band is 105 °C?
A connector pulls heat out of the joint, so the thermal side needs margin, not the bare minimum.
Preheat and contact time carry the fill, and both are at the weak end.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Top-side preheat (105 °C) and contact time (2.0 s) are the weak settings.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which two numbers in the record sit at the bottom of their windows?
steps.explanation: Pot temperature is mid-window and flux is the right family for this board, so neither explains anything. Preheat at 105 °C is in the lower half of the 90-120 °C band and contact time is at the 2.0 s floor, on a part that conducts heat away from the joint. A theory that needs a defect in the material ignores two settings that are already at the weak end of the only windows the course gives.

steps.prompt: The bridge on J-02 spans 3.20 mm across a 2.54 mm pitch. How many pitches does the bridge cover? Two decimals.
hints: One pitch is the centre-to-centre distance between adjacent pins.
1.26 pitches: it reaches past the neighbour.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 1.26 pitches: the bridge is not a whisker, it is a pool.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the span by the pitch; the units cancel.
steps.explanation: 3.20 / 2.54 = 1.26. A bridge that covers more than one pitch is a volume and drainage problem, not a fine-pitch whisker: solder sat on the board long enough to pool between two pads. On the same board, one joint is short and the neighbour is flooded, which is what uneven wetting and drainage looks like.

steps.prompt: One joint is short and its neighbour is flooded on the same pass. What does that pair of findings point to?

options.text: A single cause: the pot is too cold, so some joints do not fill and some flood.
A wetting and drainage problem around one component: the joint that did not reach temperature stayed short, and solder pooled where drainage was poor.
Two unrelated random defects; no action is possible.
A bad batch of connectors, since both findings are on the same part.

hints: A cold pot would make every joint worse, and the record says the pot is not cold.
Short fill and a pool on the same connector come from an uneven thermal and flow field, not from the solder temperature.
The mechanism has to explain both findings at once, or it is not the mechanism.
steps.feedbackCorrect: An uneven thermal and drainage field around one component: one pin too cold to fill, its neighbour with nowhere to drain.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which explanation accounts for a short barrel and a flooded neighbour at the same time?
steps.explanation: A cold pot affects the whole board, and the other joints on this board fill to 76.3-82.5 %. Two findings two pins apart on the same part are a local thermal and flow problem: the connector shields the wave and pulls heat from its own joints, so one barrel stalls while solder pools where it cannot drain. Naming one mechanism that explains both findings is the difference between a fix and an experiment.

steps.prompt: Which single change should be made first, so that its effect can be measured?

options.text: Raise the pot temperature from 255 to 270 °C and shorten the contact time.
Raise top-side preheat within the 90-120 °C band and lengthen contact toward the middle of the 2-4 s window, then re-run one board and re-measure.
Change the flux to water-soluble and keep every other setting.
Add a pallet and keep every setting, so the board is supported better.

hints: One change at a time is what makes the next measurement mean something.
The two weak settings are thermal: preheat and contact time.
Raise preheat, lengthen contact inside the window, re-run one board.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Raise preheat and lengthen contact inside their windows, one board, then re-measure.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which change touches the settings the record already flags as weak?
steps.explanation: Preheat and contact time are the two settings at the weak end and they act on the same mechanism: heat in the barrel and time for solder to climb. Changing flux, pallet and pot at once makes the result unattributable, and 270 °C is above the course's 250-260 °C SAC305 window with no evidence that heat is the binding constraint. One change, one board, one measurement is how a wave process is qualified.

steps.prompt: The first-article sheet covers every pin of the connector. What percentage of its joints is nonconforming against the 75 % minimum? One decimal.
hints: The denominator is every joint on the sheet, not only the ones that failed.
Count the rows first: the connector has twenty joints.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 5.0 % of the connector's joints: one pin in twenty.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the failing joints by the joints inspected.
steps.explanation: 1 / 20 = 5.0 %. On a sample this small a single joint is five percent, which is why first-article acceptance is per joint and why a run of three boards is not a process capability study. The number is small and the joint is still a defect.

steps.prompt: The supplier asks whether the whole lot should be rejected. What does the record support?

options.text: Reject the lot: one nonconforming joint condemns every board.
Contain the boards that have run, fix the process settings, re-qualify with a first article, and judge the lot against the re-qualified process rather than against one joint.
Release the lot: 5 % of one connector is trivial.
Release the lot and inspect 100 % by eye, since the defect is visible.

hints: A single joint is evidence about the process, not a measurement of the lot.
Containment first, then a process fix, then re-qualification: the same order as an 8D.
The lot is judged against the corrected process, not against the finding that started the investigation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Contain what has run, fix the settings, re-qualify the process, then judge the lot.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which decision does one joint actually support: a lot verdict, or a process verdict?
steps.explanation: One joint on a three-board first article is a process signal. Containment holds the boards that ran, the settings get corrected and proven on a first article, and only then does the lot get judged. Rejecting everything on one joint is as unjustified as releasing everything on 5 %, and a 100 % visual check cannot measure barrel fill: the short barrel is on the underside of the joint.

Pot margin over liquidus computed and judged against the SAC305 window
Weak settings identified from the record, not assumed
Bridge span expressed in pitches
One mechanism named that explains both findings
One change at a time, inside the published windows
Nonconforming share computed on joints, not boards
Lot decision separated from the process decision

cases.title: AOI audit: a 70 % true-call rate that still let 18 defects through
scenario: Board X ran twelve thousand boards through AOI. The audit log for four windows is in aoi-audit.csv: boards inspected, calls raised, calls verified, true defects, false calls and the defects found later by test, X-ray and visual audit.

The line reads the numbers optimistically: most of the calls were real, so the program is good. Quality has the opposite worry: eighteen defects left the line after AOI, and one of the X-ray follow-ups on a BGA ball looks bad.
Compute the three rates that matter, say what they do and do not prove, and judge the ball in xray-bga.csv against the applicable limit.

dataFiles.note: One row per review window. true_calls + false_calls = verified_calls, and verified calls are a subset of the calls raised; escapes are defects AOI did not call that were found later.

steps.prompt: What was the verification coverage, in percent: verified calls over the calls AOI raised? One decimal.
hints: Coverage is about the calls that were reviewed, not about the boards.
Add the verified_calls column and divide by the calls column.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 83.3 % of the calls were verified; the remaining 60 were never looked at.
steps.feedbackWrong: Verified calls over total calls, from the columns in the audit log.
steps.explanation: 300 of 360 calls were verified, so coverage is 83.3 %. That number matters more than it looks: every rate computed from the verified subset is an estimate for the whole population, and the 60 unverified calls are an unknown. A false-call rate quoted without its coverage is a number with no error bar.

steps.prompt: What is the false-call rate among verified calls, in percent? One decimal.
hints: The denominator is the calls that were verified, not the calls raised.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 30.0 % of verified calls were good boards.
steps.feedbackWrong: False calls over verified calls; the raised calls belong in coverage, not here.
steps.explanation: 90 of 300 verified calls were false, so 30.0 %. Not 25 % (that would divide by the 360 raised) and not 0.75 % (that would divide by the boards). Three different denominators give three different-looking programs out of the same week, which is why the definition has to travel with the number.

steps.prompt: What is the escape rate at board level, in percent? Give two decimals.
hints: Escape rate is defects found after AOI over the units inspected.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.15 % of boards carried a defect AOI did not call.
steps.feedbackWrong: Defects found later, over boards inspected: not over the calls.
steps.explanation: 18 / 12,000 = 0.15 %. That is the number a customer will ask for, and it is a board rate: it says nothing about which joint failed. The same 18 defects could sit in 18 boards at one joint each, or in one board at 18 joints, and a joint-level escape rate would answer a different question.

steps.prompt: Quality wants the escape rate against the defects AOI actually caught. Using verified true calls and escapes, what is that rate, in percent? One decimal.
hints: The denominator is the opportunities AOI judged: true calls plus escapes.
210 true calls, 18 escapes.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 7.9 % of the judged defects escaped AOI.
steps.feedbackWrong: True calls are the verified calls minus the false calls; add the escapes to them.
steps.explanation: 210 true calls plus 18 escapes is 228 found defects, so 18 / 228 = 7.9 %. This is the share of defects that AOI missed, and it is two orders of magnitude larger than the board-level rate. Both are true; they answer different questions, and reporting only the flattering one is how an escape problem stays invisible.

steps.prompt: Using the audit rows, 210 of the 300 verified calls were real defects and 90 were not. What is the correct reading of that result?

options.text: Accept the program: a 70 % true-call rate is a good result on its own.
The program still has a 30 % false-call rate that costs review capacity and a 7.9 % escape rate on judged defects; the true-call rate alone proves neither capacity nor coverage.
Reject the program: any escape means AOI is not fit for purpose.
Tighten every threshold until the escape rate is zero.

hints: A true-call rate is one ratio; the cost of review and the cost of escapes are two others.
False calls consume operator attention, and attention is what makes a 30 % rate dangerous.
Judge the program on false calls, escapes and coverage together, not on the flattering ratio.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Only 70 % of verified calls were real defects, 90 false calls burn reviewer attention, and 7.9 % of judged defects escaped.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which two costs does the true-call rate leave out?
steps.explanation: A 70 % true-call rate is arithmetic, not a verdict. The same week produced 90 false calls that had to be reviewed by hand and 18 defects that left the line. False calls are not free: they train operators to clear calls quickly, which is exactly how the next escape happens. Tightening every threshold to chase zero escapes moves the cost to review capacity and, at some point, to people dismissing calls without looking. The program is judged on all three rates and on what the customer needs.

steps.prompt: Ball A1 measures 0.45 mm and carries two voids, 0.28 mm and 0.14 mm. What is the cumulative void area as a percentage of the ball area? One decimal.
hints: Area scales with the square of the diameter, so two voids do not add as diameters.
Sum the void areas first, then divide by the ball area.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 48.4 % of the ball area — nearly double the limit.
steps.feedbackWrong: Sum the void areas, not the diameters, and divide by the full ball area.
steps.explanation: The voids have radii 0.14 mm and 0.07 mm, so their areas are pi*0.0196 = 0.0616 mm2 and pi*0.0049 = 0.0154 mm2, 0.0770 mm2 together. The ball has radius 0.225 mm and an area of pi*0.0506 = 0.1590 mm2. 0.0770 / 0.1590 = 48.4 %, which is nearly twice the 25 % limit. The arithmetic shortcut is to divide squares of diameters, since pi cancels: (0.28^2 + 0.14^2) / 0.45^2 gives the same 48.4 %. What the step is really testing is that two voids add as areas: adding the diameters would give a plausible and wrong 42 %.

steps.prompt: Against the 25 % per-ball criterion, what is the disposition of ball A1?

options.text: Accept: the largest single void is 0.28 mm, which is under half the ball.
Reject the ball: the cumulative void area is far above 25 % of the ball area, and the criterion counts cumulative area per ball, not the largest void.
Accept: voids at the ball edge drain better than central voids.
Accept and average the four balls: the array as a whole is under 25 %.

hints: The criterion is cumulative projected area per ball, in an X-ray image.
Two voids both count; the diameter of the larger one is not the measure.
A ball over the limit fails on its own, whatever the rest of the array reads.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Reject the ball: cumulative void area is well over 25 %, and the limit is per ball.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which of the four numbers in the sentence is the criterion written against?
steps.explanation: The limit is cumulative projected void area against ball area, per ball, and A1 is far over it. Comparing one void's diameter with the ball's diameter is a different calculation that happens to look reassuring. Edge location is a reliability concern on top of the area, not a credit against it, and averaging across the array would let a failing ball hide behind three good ones — the same averaging error as in m06 and m08.

steps.prompt: Ball A2 carries one 0.10 mm void in a 0.45 mm ball. What is its void percentage? One decimal.
hints: With circular voids in one ball, the area ratio is the square of the diameter ratio.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 4.9 %: a void this size is inside the limit, not a defect.
steps.feedbackWrong: Square the diameter ratio; the pi cancels.
steps.explanation: (0.10 / 0.45)^2 = 0.0494, so 4.9 %. Small central voids are common and the criterion is not a zero-void rule: chasing a void-free joint costs rework and heat cycles and buys nothing the standard asks for. The judgement is A1 fails and A2 passes, on the same board, which is what per-ball criteria are for.

steps.prompt: What does the X-ray finding change about the AOI program?

options.text: Nothing: voids under a BGA are invisible to AOI, so it is a separate issue.
It confirms the escape question: AOI cannot see under the package, so the hidden-joint sample has to be defined in the program rather than assumed to be covered by the AOI call rate.
It means AOI should be replaced by X-ray on every board.
It means the AOI thresholds were too loose and must be tightened.

hints: Ask what AOI can physically see: component presence, fillet shape, exposed joints.
A BGA ball is behind the package, so no AOI threshold reaches it.
The program's coverage claim has to name the method that covers each defect class.
steps.feedbackCorrect: It defines a gap in coverage: hidden joints need their own sample, not a tighter AOI threshold.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which defect classes in this case could AOI never have called?
steps.explanation: AOI sees what the camera sees, and a BGA ball is under the package. The 18 escapes and the failed ball are the same lesson from two directions: the program's coverage claim has to be written per defect class, with X-ray or another method named for the hidden ones. Tightening AOI thresholds cannot find a void under an opaque package, and X-raying every board is a cost decision, not a threshold decision.

steps.prompt: The failing ball is on the same Board X assembly that already carries the 8D from the AOI case. What belongs in that 8D, on this evidence?

options.text: An action to tighten the AOI void threshold, since AOI is the inspection step.
A containment of the affected boards plus a process action on the reflow and paste side, with the X-ray sample defined so the escape is measured rather than assumed.
A note that voids are normal and no action is needed.
An action to reject the whole lot on one ball.

hints: An AOI threshold cannot see a void under the package, so it cannot be the action.
The 8D needs containment, a cause on the process, and a measurement that will show whether the action worked.
Contain, act on the process, define the X-ray sample that measures the escape.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Containment, a process action on reflow and paste, and an X-ray sample that measures the escape.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which of these actions could actually change the void percentage?
steps.explanation: A void forms inside the joint during reflow: paste chemistry, profile and the escape path for volatiles decide its size, so the process action lives on that side. AOI cannot see it at all, so a tighter AOI threshold changes nothing. Containment holds the boards already built, and the X-ray sample is what turns 'we re-inspected' into a number the 8D can be closed against — the same rule m14 applies when it refuses to close an 8D on an improvement instead of the agreed metric.

rubric.criterion: Coverage computed on calls, with its consequence stated
False-call rate computed on verified calls, not on raised calls
Board-level escape rate computed on boards
Escape rate against judged defects computed on a matching denominator
Program judged on false calls, escapes and coverage together
Cumulative void area computed per ball, not from the largest void
Ball rejected on the per-ball criterion, not averaged over the array
Hidden-joint gap named as a coverage problem, not a threshold problem
8D action placed on the process, with a sample that measures the escape

cases.title: Rework record: a connector joint, a nicked trace and a hand-held iron
scenario: The short-filled J-01 from the wave case is reworked by hand on a Class 2 Board X assembly. The record in rework-record.csv carries the setpoint, the preheat, the dwell of each contact and what the operator measured afterwards: one trace nicked while the connector came off, and one joint that needed three contacts.

Two decisions are waiting. The first is the trace: the drawing sets a minimum width of 0.280 mm, and the trace measures 0.248 mm after the nick. The second is the thermal budget: three contacts on one joint, and a row where the first contact produced no solder flow at all.
Judge the repair against the class, then say what the record has to contain so the next engineer can reproduce the result.

dataFiles.name: rework-record.csv
dataFiles.note: One row per assembly. There is one dwell column per contact, so the total iron time is a sum over the row; dry_flag marks a contact that produced no solder flow.
dataFiles.content:
assembly,operation,tip,setpoint_c,preheat_c,contacts,dwell1_s,dwell2_s,dwell3_s,trace_drawn_mm,trace_min_mm,trace_after_mm,dry_flag
B-07,J-01 rework,chisel 1.2 mm,345,95,3,2.6,0.4,0.2,0.300,0.280,0.248,0
B-08,J-01 rework,chisel 1.2 mm,345,95,2,2.2,0.1,0.0,0.300,0.280,0.280,1
B-09,J-01 rework,chisel 1.2 mm,345,95,1,2.4,0.0,0.0,0.300,0.280,0.280,0

steps.prompt: B-07 ran at a 345 °C setpoint. Against the course's hand-soldering band of 330-360 °C, how does that setpoint read?

options.text: Too cold for lead-free and a likely cause of the cold joint.
Inside the band, near its middle: the setpoint is defensible, so the cause of the short fill is elsewhere in the budget.
Too hot, and above every published limit for SAC305.
Irrelevant, because only the measured joint temperature matters.

hints: The course band for hand soldering lead-free is 330-360 °C, and J-STD-001 does not fix one number for every joint.
345 sits between 330 and 360.
The setpoint is inside the band, so it is not the defect.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 345 °C is inside the 330-360 °C band: the setpoint is not what went wrong.
steps.feedbackWrong: Compare the setpoint with the band the lesson gives, not with a number from memory.
steps.explanation: 345 °C sits in the middle of the course's 330-360 °C band, and published sources are looser still: IPC-7711 procedures start at about 315 °C and say to change it as necessary, vendor tables quote up to 400 °C for lead-free. So the setpoint is not the defect, and 'raise the temperature' is not a diagnosis. The setpoint is also only half the budget: contact time, preheat and how many times the joint is heated decide the outcome.

steps.prompt: B-07 was heated for dwells of 2.6, 0.4 and 0.2 s. What is the total iron time on the board, in seconds? One decimal.
hints: The budget counts every contact, not only the successful one.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 3.2 s in total: the successful contact plus two more the record kept.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add every dwell in the row, including the ones that produced nothing.
steps.explanation: 2.6 + 0.4 + 0.2 = 3.2 s. A single 2.6 s contact is unremarkable; 3.2 s across three contacts means the joint was brought to temperature, lost it, and was brought up again. Repeated heating grows the intermetallic layer and stresses the pad, which is why the count of contacts belongs in the record next to the dwell.

steps.prompt: The iron delivers about 45 W during contact. How much energy went into the board on B-07, in joules?
hints: Energy is power times time.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 144 J of iron time on one joint.
steps.feedbackWrong: Multiply the total seconds by the power; J = W x s.
steps.explanation: 45 W for 3.2 s is 144 J. This is the number to put in the record beside the setpoint: a joint that took 144 J is a joint with a thermal problem — a ground plane, a cold preheat, or a tip too small for the pad — and not a joint that needed a hotter setpoint. It becomes the baseline for the next board, which is the whole point of recording a thermal budget.

steps.prompt: The drawing sets a minimum conductor width of 0.280 mm. The nicked trace measures 0.248 mm. What is the width reduction against that minimum, in percent? One decimal.
hints: The limit is written against the minimum width on the drawing, not the as-drawn width.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 11.4 %: inside Class 2, outside Class 3.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loss over the minimum width: 0.032 mm on a 0.280 mm trace.
steps.explanation: 0.032 / 0.280 = 11.4 %. The denominator matters more than the numerator. The same 0.248 mm trace passes a Class 2 limit of 20 % and fails a Class 3 limit of 10 %, because IPC-A-600 caps the reduction of the minimum conductor width the drawing already fixes. Dividing by the as-drawn 0.300 mm would give a flattering 17.3 % and still pass Class 2, which is exactly why the standard names the minimum and not the nominal.

steps.prompt: What is the narrowest that trace may become and still meet the Class 2 limit, in mm?
hints: Turn the percentage into a width: the limit is 20 % of the 0.280 mm minimum.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.224 mm is the floor for Class 2 on this drawing.
steps.feedbackWrong: Subtract the allowed loss from the minimum width, or multiply by (1 - 20 %).
steps.explanation: 0.280 mm less 20 % is 0.224 mm. The board measures 0.248 mm, so it passes with 0.024 mm to spare, a real margin rather than a rounding one. That margin is what the record protects: a repair judged by eye as slightly thinner has no way of saying whether it sits 0.024 mm inside the limit or 0.024 mm outside it.

steps.prompt: The same repair on a Class 3 board would be judged against 10 %. What is the narrowest acceptable width there, in mm?
hints: Class 3 allows a tenth of the minimum width, not a fifth.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 0.252 mm on Class 3: the same 0.248 mm trace would fail there.
steps.feedbackWrong: Multiply the minimum width by (1 - 10 %).
steps.explanation: 0.280 x 0.90 = 0.252 mm. At 0.248 mm the trace is 0.004 mm under the Class 3 floor, so the identical physical repair passes Class 2 and fails Class 3 by four microns. That is why the class has to be on the record before the repair: it is set by the product, not by how bad the nick looks, and at this margin nothing but the number separates the two answers.

steps.prompt: What is the disposition of the trace on B-07, a Class 2 board?

options.text: Accept: 20 % is at the limit, not over it, and the record shows the measurement.
Reject the board: any nick during rework is a repair and repairs are not allowed.
Accept and do not record it, since the board still works.
Accept on Class 3 limits, which are looser.

hints: The limit is a maximum reduction, so anything under it passes.
Class 2 allows 20 %; the board measured 11.4 %.
Accept, and record the measurement, the denominator and the class it was judged against.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Accept: 11.4 % is inside the 20 % limit, and both numbers go in the record.
steps.feedbackWrong: Is the measured reduction over the limit for the class this board actually is?
steps.explanation: 11.4 % against a 20 % limit passes with margin. Recording it is what makes the acceptance durable: a year later the board either has a line that says '0.248 mm against a 0.280 mm minimum, 11.4 %, Class 2 limit 20 %' or it has nothing, and 'it still works' is not a record. Class 3 would have made the same measurement a defect at 0.252 mm, so the class is part of the finding and not a detail of the paperwork.

steps.prompt: B-08 shows dry_flag 1 on its first contact and two contacts in total. What does that row say about the process, rather than about the operator?

options.text: Nothing: a dry contact is an operator error and is not a process signal.
The joint needed more heat than one contact could deliver, so the preheat, tip size or board support is loading the joint beyond the budget — the same thermal question the wave case raised.
The setpoint was too low and should be raised for every joint.
The solder wire was the wrong diameter.

hints: A contact that produced no flow means the joint was not at temperature.
Two contacts on the same joint is a repeat of the m08 finding: the thermal path is the constraint.
Fix the heat path, not the setpoint for every joint on the line.
steps.feedbackCorrect: The joint is thermally loaded: preheat, tip size or support, not a global setpoint change.
steps.feedbackWrong: What is the difference between 'this joint is hard to heat' and 'the iron is too cold'?
steps.explanation: A dry contact is the record's way of saying the joint was not at wetting temperature, and the second contact is the recovery. Raising the setpoint for the whole line would overheat every easy joint to rescue one hard one; the m08 case reached the same conclusion from the wave side. The fix is in the heat path — preheat the board, use a tip that matches the pad, support the board — and the record is what shows the fix worked on the next one.

steps.prompt: What has to be in the rework record for the next engineer to reproduce this result?

options.text: The pass/fail verdict and the operator's initials.
Required class, setpoint, tip, preheat, dwells and number of contacts, measured trace width with the limit it was judged against, and the inspection result.
The serial number and the date, because the process is standard.
A photograph of the joint, since numbers cannot describe solder.

hints: Reproducing a result needs the settings, the measurements and the standard they were judged against.
A verdict without the numbers cannot be re-judged when the class or the standard changes.
Class, settings, measurements, limits, result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Class, settings, measurements, the limit each was judged against, and the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which of these could another engineer use to reach the same decision without asking you?
steps.explanation: A record that says 'passed' cannot be re-judged when the product class changes or the standard moves from Rev C to Rev D, and that is exactly what happened to this course's own source. Class, setpoint, tip, preheat, dwells, contact count, the measured width against the minimum it was compared with, and the inspection result make the decision reproducible. A photo is useful evidence and not a substitute for the numbers.

rubric.criterion: Setpoint judged against the band, not against a remembered number
Thermal budget counted over every contact
Energy in joules derived from power and time
Conductor reduction measured against the drawing width
Class 2 width floor computed from the percentage limit
Class 3 floor computed and the same repair shown to fail there
Disposition at the limit accepted with the measurement recorded
Dry contact read as a thermal-load signal, not as a setpoint problem
Record contents named so the decision can be re-judged

cases.title: AOI over-rejection on Board X: DPMO, sampling scope and an 8D that is not closed
scenario: Board X runs 1,240 boards a day with 620 solder opportunities per board. Last week AOI raised 47 calls against the BGA and the fine-pitch QFP; the defect review confirmed 38 of them and threw 9 out as false calls.

The 8D team contained the suspect lot and needs a sampling plan for the retroactive search: one lot is 3,000 boards, another is 5,000. The control plan requires ISO 2859-1 general inspection level II at AQL 1.0.
A corrective action has been running for six weeks on a different defect family: 96 defects in 6,000 boards before, 21 defects in 7,500 boards after. The agreed effectiveness target is 1,000 ppm.
Compute the metrics the 8D needs, and be honest about what the numbers do and do not prove.

dataFiles.name: defect-log.csv
dataFiles.content:
family,calls,confirmed,false_calls,boards_in_window
BGA void / non-wet,47,38,9,1240
QFP bridging,0,0,0,1240

steps.prompt: Compute DPMO for Board X from the confirmed defects. DPMO = defects / (boards x opportunities per board) x 1,000,000. One decimal.
hints: Use confirmed defects, not AOI calls.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 49.4 DPMO — computed from confirmed defects only.
steps.feedbackWrong: Multiply boards by opportunities first, then divide, then scale to a million.
steps.explanation: 38 / (1,240 x 620) = 38 / 768,800 = 4.94 x 10^-5, which is 49.4 defects per million opportunities. Using the 47 AOI calls instead would inflate the number to about 61 DPMO and turn an inspection problem into a process problem.

steps.prompt: AOI raised 47 calls of which 38 were confirmed. What is the false-call rate, in percent? One decimal.
hints: The false calls are the calls that did not survive review.
47 - 38 = 9 false calls out of 47 calls.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 19.1 % false calls — an inspection capability issue, not a solder issue.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the false calls by the total calls, not by the confirmed defects.
steps.explanation: 9 / 47 = 19.1 %. The course treats false calls as a separate metric from escape rate: a high false-call rate costs review time and erodes trust in the station, but it does not put a bad board in the field the way an escape does.

steps.prompt: For a lot of 3,000 boards, what is the ISO 2859-1 code letter at general inspection level II?

options.text: J
K
L
M

hints: The lot-size ranges for level II step at 1,200 and at 3,200.
3,000 falls in the 1,201-3,200 band.
That band is code K: n = 125 at AQL 1.0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Code K for 3,000 boards: sample 125, Ac 3, Re 4.
steps.feedbackWrong: Find the lot-size band first; the letter follows from the band, not from the count.
steps.explanation: At general inspection level II a lot of 3,000 sits in the 1,201-3,200 band, which is code K: 125 pieces sampled, accept at 3, reject at 4 for AQL 1.0. Code L belongs to the next band (3,201-10,000) and code J to the one below (501-1,200).

steps.prompt: For that 3,000-board lot at code K, AQL 1.0, how many pieces are sampled?
hints: Code K fixes the sample size.
It is the n column for K, not a percentage of the lot.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 125 pieces sampled.
steps.feedbackWrong: This is a table lookup for code K at AQL 1.0.
steps.explanation: Code K samples 125 pieces. The accept number is 3 and the reject number 4, so finding 3 or fewer nonconforming units accepts the lot and 4 rejects it — the plan is not a zero-defect rule.

steps.prompt: The retroactive search on the 3,000-board lot finds 3 nonconforming boards. What does the plan say?

options.text: Reject the lot: any nonconformity in a containment sample fails it.
Accept the lot against this plan (Ac = 3) — acceptance sampling qualifies the lot, not the process, so the 8D stays open until the ppm target is met.
Accept the lot and close the 8D.
Reject and double the sample until zero defects are found.

hints: Ac is the acceptance number for the plan, and it is not zero.
Ac = 3 means 3 or fewer accepts; Re = 4 is the reject threshold.
Accepting the lot on the sampling plan does not close the 8D.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Accept against Ac = 3, and keep the 8D open — sampling says nothing about the cause.
steps.feedbackWrong: Separate the sampling decision from the corrective-action decision.
steps.explanation: At AQL 1.0 code K the acceptance number is 3, so three nonconforming boards accept the lot. That is a statement about the lot against an agreed quality level, not evidence that the cause is fixed: acceptance sampling with Ac > 0 always passes some nonconforming units, which is why the 8D is closed on the effectiveness metric, not on the sample.

steps.prompt: The second lot is 5,000 boards at the same level and AQL. How many pieces does the plan sample?
hints: 5,000 falls in the 3,201-10,000 band.
That band is code L.
Code L samples 200 pieces: Ac 5, Re 6.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 200 pieces at code L (Ac 5, Re 6).
steps.feedbackWrong: Find the band for 5,000 first, then read n for that code.
steps.explanation: 5,000 boards is code L, which samples 200 pieces with Ac 5 and Re 6 at AQL 1.0. Note that the sample grows far more slowly than the lot: doubling the lot from 3,000 to 5,000 raises the sample from 125 to 200, which is why sampling alone cannot bound a large escape.

steps.prompt: Corrective-action window: 96 defects in 6,000 boards. What is that rate in ppm?
hints: ppm is defects per million boards.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 16,000 ppm before the action.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide defects by boards, then multiply by a million.
steps.explanation: 96 / 6,000 = 0.016, which is 16,000 defects per million boards. Stating it in ppm rather than percent keeps the comparison with the 1,000 ppm target in one scale.

steps.prompt: After the action: 21 defects in 7,500 boards. What is the rate in ppm?
hints: Same conversion as the before figure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 2,800 ppm after the action.
steps.feedbackWrong: Defects over boards, then scale to a million.
steps.explanation: 21 / 7,500 = 0.0028, so 2,800 ppm. The two windows are different lengths, which is exactly why the comparison is made on a rate and not on a defect count.

steps.prompt: What is the reduction between the two rates, in percent? One decimal.
hints: Reduction is measured against the before rate.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 82.5 % reduction — a real improvement, and still not the target.
steps.feedbackWrong: Divide the improvement by the before rate, then multiply by 100.
steps.explanation: (16,000 - 2,800) / 16,000 = 82.5 %. An 82.5 % reduction sounds like success until it is put against the target: 2,800 ppm is still nearly three times the agreed 1,000 ppm, so by the metric the course uses the action is not yet effective.

steps.prompt: The effectiveness target is 1,000 ppm and the after rate is 2,800 ppm. What is the correct 8D status?

options.text: Close the 8D: an 82.5 % reduction is a passing result.
Keep the 8D open: the action improved the rate but did not reach the agreed metric, so effectiveness is not demonstrated.
Close the 8D and open a new one for the residual 2,800 ppm.
Change the target to 3,000 ppm so the action passes.

hints: Effectiveness is judged against the metric agreed before the action.
The course closes an 8D on the metric, not on the improvement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Keep it open — the improvement is real, the target is not met.
steps.feedbackWrong: Which number was agreed before the action started?
steps.explanation: An 82.5 % improvement with a residual rate nearly three times the target is a partial result. The course's rule is that the 8D stays open until the effectiveness metric is met with evidence; renegotiating the target after the fact destroys the point of having one, and opening a second 8D for the same cause just moves the paperwork.
